results.source: Postuma RB et al., Mov Disord 2015;30(12):1591-1601
results.summary: Clinically established Parkinson's disease requires: (1) parkinsonism defined as bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity; (2) absence of absolute exclusion criteria (e.g., cerebellar signs, downward vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, presynaptic dopamine system imaging showing normal binding); (3) at least two supportive criteria (dramatic beneficial response to dopaminergic therapy, levodopa-induced dyskinesia, rest tremor of a limb, olfactory loss, or cardiac sympathetic denervation on MIBG); and (4) no red flags. The criteria distinguish clinically established from clinically probable PD.
results.title: MDS Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson's Disease

results.source: Tolosa E et al., Lancet Neurol 2021;20:385-397
results.summary: Up to 20-25% of clinically diagnosed PD cases lack pathological confirmation at autopsy, highlighting ongoing diagnostic challenges. Key mimics include essential tremor, drug-induced parkinsonism, vascular parkinsonism, MSA, and PSP. DaTscan imaging supports the diagnosis of presynaptic dopaminergic loss and distinguishes degenerative parkinsonism from essential tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism; it cannot distinguish idiopathic PD from MSA or PSP.
results.title: Challenges in the Diagnosis of Parkinson's Disease

results.source: Marshall VL et al., Mov Disord 2009;24:500-508
results.summary: In cases of clinical uncertainty, DaTscan (FP-CIT SPECT) demonstrated high sensitivity for detecting presynaptic dopaminergic deficit. Patients with clinically uncertain parkinsonism and abnormal DaTscan had a high rate of pathologically confirmed neurodegeneration at follow-up. DaTscan should be reserved for cases where clinical diagnosis is uncertain, not used routinely when clinical criteria are met.
results.title: Parkinson's Disease is Overdiagnosed Clinically at Baseline in Diagnostically Uncertain Cases

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Nasser is a 56-year-old left-handed Lebanese-American Arabic language instructor who presents to the outpatient movement disorders clinic with a 14-month history of progressive right hand tremor, stiffness, and slowing of fine motor movements. The patient first noticed an intermittent trembling in her right hand approximately 14 months ago while resting her hand in her lap during a faculty meeting. The tremor was initially subtle and occurred only at rest; she was not initially concerned and attributed it to stress. Over the following months the tremor became more persistent and she noticed it particularly when walking, with her right hand shaking while her left arm swung normally.

Over the past year, she has experienced worsening right hand stiffness and slowness that has significantly affected her work. As an Arabic language instructor who demonstrates calligraphy techniques to students, she has noticed that her right-hand writing has become progressively smaller and more cramped, with letters deteriorating toward the end of a line. She has reduced her teaching hours partly because she can no longer write fluidly on the whiteboard. She reports that buttoning the right cuff of her blouse has become slow and difficult, and that she now takes about twice as long as before to prepare meals due to right hand clumsiness. Her husband has noticed that her voice has become softer and her facial expression less animated over the past six months.

The patient denies any history of exposure to antipsychotics, antiemetics (specifically metoclopramide or prochlorperazine), or other dopamine-blocking agents. She has been taking topiramate for migraine prophylaxis for three years, which predates her motor symptoms by over two years and has not changed in dose. She denies any history of encephalitis, head trauma, or known toxin exposure including pesticides or heavy metals.

Her subclinical hypothyroidism was identified on routine bloodwork 14 months ago (TSH 5.8 mIU/L, free T4 normal at 1.1 ng/dL). Her endocrinologist elected to monitor without treatment given the borderline elevation and absence of symptoms at that time. She was told her fatigue and mild cognitive slowing could be related to the thyroid finding. The patient is now uncertain whether her motor symptoms could be thyroid-related.

She denies visual hallucinations, vivid dream enactment, or acting out dreams during sleep. She endorses mild constipation over the past year (2-3 bowel movements per week) and reports decreased sense of smell that she first noticed approximately 18 months ago. She denies significant orthostatic symptoms, urinary urgency, or incontinence. She denies falls but has had two near-fall episodes in the past four months when turning quickly.

Family history is notable for her father, now 82 years old, who was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease at age 74 and is on carbidopa-levodopa with good response.
